title: Did it really originate from bartering?
aliases: The controversy about the origins of money
source: 用户提供截图 · 鸭圈原文核对
articleHtml:
A

The arguments put forward by Alfred Mitchell-Innes in a paper entitled What is Money?, published in the 1913 edition of The Banking Law Journal, have only relatively recently attracted the attention they deserve. In this paper, Mitchell-Innes, a British diplomat then living in the US, reviewed the history and usage of money. On both historical and logical grounds, he asserted that the modern science of political economy rested on a series of assumptions regarding money and credit that were false. One of the most important of these assumptions was the belief that in primitive societies, before the invention of money and a banking system, people relied on barter, exchanging goods and services even before selling them. This theory and the existence of a barter economy had been the commonly held view ever since it was promoted by the renowned Scottish economist Adam Smith in his 1776 work The Wealth of Nations.

B

Adam Smith's explanation appears in countless textbooks on economics, partly because it is a convenient story that seems to make sense to students. This has helped to transform the myth of the barter system into historical fact. It goes something like this. Long ago, before the invention of money, goods were simply traded for other goods. Without money, trade was only possible if there was a double coincidence of needs. If one person grew and sold potatoes and the other makes shoes, they will only engage in exchange if the one selling shoes needs potatoes and the one selling potatoes needs a new pair of shoes.

C

The problem with this barter system is that, even if they each have a surplus of the goods they wish to sell, no trade will occur unless the potential buyer has something which the seller needs. For Smith, it seemed logical that people had to deal with this problem by using a specific commodity – perhaps gold or silver – to serve as money that could be used to purchase other goods and services. Economists refer to this monetary function as a 'medium of exchange'. The need for money may become even more apparent when dealing with perishable goods such as bread or meat. For example, a butcher may have more meat in his shop than he can consume. If he doesn't find someone to buy it, his meat will spoil. For Smith and his followers, this illustrates the need for money as a means of storing wealth, as well as a medium of exchange. For example, if the butcher could exchange his excess meat for money, he could spend that money one month or one year later when he finally needed more shoes. Even more importantly, once a butcher can exchange his excess meat for money, he is encouraged to work harder, longer and more efficiently so as to produce more and more excess meat that he can exchange for more money that will store the value of his excess production safely. The implication of this argument is that without money, it would be inefficient and even unwise to over-produce, since most over-production would simply go to waste. It has seemed unjustifiably logical to many economists that money is therefore conducive and even necessary to foster hard work, over-production, profits and a prosperous society.

D

It was this traditional story that Mitchell-Innes challenged over one hundred years ago. He asserted that the barter theory that emerged from Smith contradicts both logic and historical fact. Smith's theory simply does not describe what happens in the real world. For example, if you grew up in a small town in the US in the 1970s, you might remember that you could go to the grocery store, pick up groceries, and simply sign a slip of paper acknowledging your receipt of the groceries. The same could be done in Smith's imagined scenario. If the shoe buyer was trustworthy, the shoe seller could simply create a record of the shoes purchased on credit by the shoe buyer, and of their value in some agreed unit of account. This is certainly not barter, and it is not a purchase using a medium of exchange. Instead it is the exchange of a commodity for a credit.

E

Although Mitchell-Innes's work received some favourable reviews at the time, most notably from John Maynard Keynes, the influential British economist, his ideas were neglected for almost 75 years until the 1990s. Since then, academic studies in economics and anthropology demonstrate that there has been a shift in thinking. Some economists now even claim that Smith's idea was only ever a 'crude model' used to simplify the context of modern economic systems, not a real theory about past ones. Despite all this, incomprehensibly, the myth continues into the 21st century, and still features in economics textbooks and the public's consciousness.

F

In his book Debt, the first 5000 years, anthropologist David Graeber asserts that where instances of barter have occurred, it wasn't as part of a purely barter economy, and money didn't emerge from it – rather, barter emerged from money. After the fall of the Roman Empire around fifteen hundred years ago, for example, Europeans used barter as a substitute for the Roman currency people had become used to. 'In most of the cases we know about, [barter] takes place between people who are familiar with the use of money, but for one reason or another, don't have a lot of it around,' explains Graeber. He and other anthropologists provide strong arguments which state that many of the examples used by economists in the past to support the view that money originated from bartering were not based on any real evidence. Caroline Humphrey's Cambridge University dissertation is regarded as the definitive anthropological work on barter. Her statement is as clear as it is emphatic: 'No example of a barter economy, pure and simple, has ever been described, let alone the emergence from it of money; all available evidence suggests there has never been such a thing.' Mitchell-Innes knew this over a century ago, yet the myth persists.
